lead: The superheterodyne receiver, or superhet, converts every incoming radio signal to one fixed intermediate frequency (IF) before detection. Why: amplifiers and filters give high gain and sharp selectivity easily at a low fixed frequency, not at every station's frequency. A local oscillator (LO) and mixer do the conversion; the radio-frequency (RF) filter before the mixer rejects the image, a second unwanted frequency that would otherwise land on the same IF. Every AM/FM radio, TV tuner and many wireless receivers uses this plan.
prereq: You need: envelope detection from Chapter 2.5, and frequency translation and band-pass filters from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Why shift to a fixed IF

blocks.text: An antenna receives many weak signals. The RF amplifier (radio-frequency amplifier) selects the wanted band and raises the signal a little. It also gives the first rejection of unwanted frequencies. RF means the incoming radio frequency; f<sub>RF</sub> is its value in hertz.

A receiver could filter and amplify directly at f<sub>RF</sub>. That is hard: the tuned circuits must move over the whole band, and high gain at high frequency can oscillate. The superheterodyne plan avoids this. A mixer and local oscillator (LO) translate every station to one fixed intermediate frequency (IF). The IF is the frequency where the receiver does most of its filtering and amplification. This plan is what some syllabi call the superhet receiver. In AM broadcast the IF is commonly 455 kHz.

The IF amplifier gives most of the gain and the IF filter gives the sharp bandwidth. Both are fixed, so they can be designed once for best performance. A detector then recovers the audio, and an audio amplifier drives the speaker. An automatic gain control (AGC) loop senses the carrier level and adjusts RF and IF gain so weak and strong stations sound similar.

sections.h3: Local oscillator, mixing and the image

blocks.text: The local oscillator runs at f<sub>LO</sub>. The mixer multiplies RF and LO, producing sum and difference frequencies. The difference is set equal to the IF, and the sum is filtered out:
High-side injection (LO above the signal): f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>,   f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub>
blocks.where: f<sub>LO</sub> is the local oscillator frequency; f<sub>RF</sub> is the wanted radio frequency; f<sub>IF</sub> is the intermediate frequency; f<sub>image</sub> is the image frequency, the unwanted second RF that also gives f<sub>IF</sub>.

blocks.text: This is high-side injection: the LO is above the signal. Then f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>RF</sub> = f<sub>IF</sub>. Low-side injection puts the LO below: f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub>, and the image becomes f<sub>RF</sub> − 2f<sub>IF</sub>. The image is a second RF that also gives f<sub>IF</sub> at the mixer output. For high-side injection, f<sub>image</sub> − f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>IF</sub>. The mixer cannot tell which one is wanted.

The RF filter before the mixer must reject the image. It passes f<sub>RF</sub> and stops f<sub>image</sub>. If the image reaches the mixer, it lands on the same IF and no later filter can separate it. The RF filter's passband therefore sets image rejection; a narrow filter near the antenna helps.

After the IF filter, the detector recovers the message. For AM this is an envelope detector, covered in Chapter 2.5. The audio amplifier raises the audio to speaker level. AGC takes a DC voltage from the detector, filters it, and feeds it back to the RF and IF amplifiers. A strong station increases AGC voltage and lowers gain; a weak station raises gain. This keeps the audio output nearly constant.

The tuning knob must move the RF filter and the LO together. When f<sub>RF</sub> changes by Δf, f<sub>LO</sub> must change by the same Δf so the difference stays at f<sub>IF</sub>. This is tracking. Alignment is the service adjustment that sets the RF and LO tuned circuits to track across the band. Small tracking errors reduce gain and image rejection at band edges. The IF alignment is set once at the factory and is not tuned by the listener.

spec.title: Superheterodyne receiver
spec.aria: The antenna signal passes through an RF amplifier to a mixer, where a local oscillator shifts it to a fixed IF; IF amplification, detection and audio output follow.

examples.question: An AM broadcast receiver has an RF signal at 1.000 MHz and an IF of 455 kHz with high-side injection. Find the local oscillator frequency and the image frequency. If the RF filter passband is 20 kHz wide around 1.000 MHz, does it reject the image?
steps: Convert: f<sub>RF</sub> = 1.000 MHz, f<sub>IF</sub> = 455 kHz = 0.455 MHz.
High-side injection: f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub> = 1.000 + 0.455 = 1.455 MHz.
Image: f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> = 1.000 + 2(0.455) = 1.000 + 0.910 = 1.910 MHz. This is also f<sub>LO</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub> = 1.455 + 0.455.

RF passband: 20 kHz = 0.020 MHz wide, so 0.990 MHz to 1.010 MHz. The image at 1.910 MHz is 0.910 MHz above the passband centre and far outside the 0.990 MHz to 1.010 MHz passband. An ideal RF filter rejects it; a real filter needs enough attenuation there.
examples.answer: f<sub>LO</sub> = 1.455 MHz and f<sub>image</sub> = 1.910 MHz; the 20 kHz RF passband does not include the image, so the RF filter rejects it.
examples.check:
f_rf = 1.000
f_if = 0.455
f_lo = f_rf + f_if
f_image = f_rf + 2 * f_if
print(f"{f_lo:.3f}")
print(f"{f_image:.3f}")

traps: The image is not the local oscillator. For high-side injection f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub>, which is also f<sub>LO</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>.
High-side and low-side injection give different f<sub>LO</sub> and different images. Do not use f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> when f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub>.
The IF is not the audio frequency. 455 kHz is the fixed band before the detector; audio is a few kHz after it.
Image rejection belongs to the RF filter before the mixer. After mixing, the image and wanted signal share the same IF.
Most gain and selectivity come from the IF stages. The RF amplifier mainly selects the band and lowers the image.

quiz.q: What is the intermediate frequency in AM broadcast receivers?
quiz.a: 455 kHz, the common AM broadcast value.

quiz.q: Why does a superhet use a fixed IF instead of high-gain tuned amplifiers at every RF?
quiz.a: A fixed IF filter and amplifier can be designed once for high gain and sharp bandwidth. Tuning high-gain RF stages over the band is harder and can oscillate.

quiz.q: An AM receiver has f<sub>RF</sub> = 800 kHz, f<sub>IF</sub> = 455 kHz and high-side injection. Find f<sub>LO</sub> and f<sub>image</sub>.
A receiver uses low-side injection. Does f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> still hold? Explain in one line.
quiz.a: No. Low-side gives f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub> and f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> − 2f<sub>IF</sub>, so the image lies below the signal.

quiz.q: A high-side receiver has f<sub>LO</sub> = 1.500 MHz and f<sub>IF</sub> = 455 kHz. Find f<sub>RF</sub> and f<sub>image</sub>.
What does AGC stand for and what does it control?
quiz.a: Automatic gain control; it adjusts RF and IF gain to keep the audio output steady.

quiz.q: Why must the image be rejected before the mixer, not after?
quiz.a: After mixing, the image and the wanted signal produce the same IF. No later filter can separate them.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern receivers often digitize the IF directly (IF sampling) or use zero-IF direct conversion, which has no image at f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> but adds DC offset and flicker noise. Image-reject mixers use two quadrature mixers to cancel the image without a sharp RF filter. Software-defined radios push the ADC closer to the antenna and do channel filtering in software. Search next for 'superheterodyne image frequency', 'IF sampling receiver' and 'image-reject mixer'.
